Points to Note
Synthesis of Current Evidence: Primary cilia may coordinate liver-gut-pancreas and brain-gut-liver axes in MASH by regulating metabolic, inflammatory, and fibrotic pathways.Major Controversies: Direct evidence in MASH remains limited, and whether ciliary dysfunction is a cause or consequence of disease is unclear.Future Directions: Studies should validate cilia-based biomarkers and test targeted therapies in MASH models and patient subgroups.

Introduction
Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is rapidly reshaping the landscape of chronic liver disease worldwide. Globally, over one-third of adults are affected by metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).[1] As a progressive stage of MASLD, MASH has become a significant driver of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC),[2] while also exacerbating the risk of cardiovascular events,[3] chronic kidney disease,[4] and neurodegenerative disorders.[5] This creates a cross-organ pathological network. Recent evidence suggests that single-target interventions are insufficient to address the complex, multi-axial pathology of MASH. However, primary cilia (PC) – organelles once regarded as “evolutionary relics” – mediate information transduction and cellular process regulation across multiple systems.[6] Consequently, the PC may serve as a critical hub for trans-systemic regulation.

Overview of PC
Cilia are microtubule-based structures, evolutionarily highly conserved, present on nearly all mammalian cells. They serve as crucial signaling hubs in energy metabolism and inflammation, participating in processes such as the cell cycle, signal transduction, and autophagy.[6] Cilia protrude from the cell surface as finger-like projections, consisting of a microtubule axoneme covered by a specialized plasma membrane anchored by a basal body or centriole. A dichotomous classification of cilia is based on motility differences arising from “9+2” to “9+0” microtubule configurations: motile cilia and non-motile cilia, the latter also termed PC.[7] The PC’s capacity for sensing and modulating information has long been recognized.[6,8] Defects in ciliary structure or function can lead to ciliopathies, whose core manifestations or major complications include metabolic diseases such as obesity and diabetes.[9]

As a significant early warning sign of metabolic syndrome,[10] MASH is associated with abnormalities in PC structure and function: the loss of cilia on hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) exacerbates fibrosis progression through multiple pathways,[11,12] while ciliary dysfunction in the intestinal system not only worsens metabolic disturbances but also promotes brain functional decline.[13] As detailed in Section 4, PCs are present in HSCs, cholangiocytes, pancreatic islets, enteric neurons, and hypothalamic neurons. These nodes position the PC as an overlapping component of relevant networks, a common pathological nexus for the microbe-metabolism-neuron axis, and a potential therapeutic target for MASH.

Pathogenesis of MASH and Evidence for PC Abnormalities
The traditional exclusion-based term “non-alcoholic” has been superseded, with MASLD and MASH now adopted as standard nomenclature. MASLD requires the presence of hepatic steatosis plus at least one cardiometabolic risk factor, while MASH additionally involves inflammation and hepatocyte ballooning.[14,15] This review uses MASLD/MASH uniformly, retaining non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)/non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) when citing pre-2023 studies.[16]

MASH is a chronic liver disease driven and progressively aggravated by metabolic dysregulation. Its core pathogenesis involves a series of pathological processes including insulin resistance (IR), lipotoxicity, oxidative stress, organelle dysfunction, and apoptosis.[17] These processes can be exacerbated by metabolic abnormalities such as obesity, hypertension, and hypertriglyceridemia.[18,19] During disease progression, lipid accumulation in hepatocytes induces mitochondrial dysfunction and excessive reactive oxygen species generation, subsequently activating the JNK pathway and endoplasmic reticulum stress. This ultimately triggers hepatocyte apoptosis through pathways such as caspase-3, further activating HSCs and promoting fibrosis.[20–22]

Notably, the PC, as a ubiquitous organelle, mediates vital physiological and pathological signals in different organs. In the liver, PCs on cholangiocytes have been established as key mechano- and chemosensors. Through proteins like polycystin-2, they perceive changes in bile composition and flow, regulating intracellular Ca2+ and cAMP balance, thereby influencing cell proliferation and secretion.[23,24] Studies show that in genetic polycystic liver disease and experimental cholestasis models, PC functional defects (e.g., downregulation of polycystin-2) can lead to aberrant activation of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling, promoting angiogenesis and inflammatory-fibrotic responses.[25] Furthermore, in fibropolycystic liver disease models, defects in cilia-associated proteins can activate β-catenin signaling, driving the expression of chemokines such as CXCL10, recruiting macrophages, and exacerbating periportal fibrosis.[26]

In biliary atresia and most fibrocystic liver diseases, bending, shortening, loss, and genetic defects of PCs have been clearly associated with disease progression.[27–29] Notably, these diseases share a hypoxic microenvironment with MASH. Existing studies have observed an association between hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1α) activation and ciliary loss in cholangiocytes.[27,30] In vitro experiments exposing cholangiocyte epithelial cells to hypoxic conditions (0.5% O2) directly reduced PC number and shortened their length. This suggests that hypoxia, a prevalent microenvironmental alteration in MASH and many chronic liver diseases,[31,32] likely causes similar physical disruption to PCs in intrahepatic cells. Therefore, hypoxia-induced PC dysfunction may be a potential mechanism for ductular reaction and fibrosis in MASH.

In a mouse model with cholangiocyte-specific knockout of the key PC gene Kif3a, PC-deficient cholangiocyte epithelial cells exhibited upregulation of senescence and DNA damage response pathway genes and downregulation of proliferation-related genes at the transcriptome level. These cells showed significantly reduced proliferative capacity and increased senescence markers (SA-β-Gal). When transplanted into injured livers, their engraftment and repair capacity were severely impaired. This indicates that PC dysfunction is sufficient to drive cells into senescence and deprive them of regenerative potential. Notably, a self-reinforcing vicious cycle exists among hypoxia, PC damage, and cellular senescence.Devarbhavi et al.,[33] showed that hypoxia can directly induce biliary epithelial cell (BEC) senescence; conversely, inducing cholangiocyte senescence significantly reduced the proportion of ciliated cells. Simultaneously, PC loss upregulated genes like HIF Hif1a. Therefore, in the pathological context of MASH, local hepatic hypoxia and metabolic stress may act as initial hits, damaging PC structure and function. Impaired PCs then push cholangiocytes or other liver cells into a senescent state. Inflammatory factors (senescence-associated secretory phenotype) secreted by senescent cells worsen the microenvironment, exacerbating hypoxia and metabolic abnormalities, and further inhibiting PC function, creating a negative feedback loop that impedes tissue repair.

Furthermore, the activated mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway in MASH has been shown to bidirectionally regulate PC dynamics; mTOR inhibition enhances autophagy and promotes ciliary elongation, whereas its activation shortens cilia.[34] Thus, mTOR dysregulation in MASH may contribute to metabolic disturbances and disruption of cellular homeostasis by affecting PCs.

However, research on the role of PCs in MASH is still in its infancy. Although the aforementioned studies in related liver disease models have identified PC involvement in key pathways regulating inflammation and fibrosis, and MASH similarly features metabolism stress-induced inflammation and fibrosis, direct experimental evidence proving that PC structural or functional changes are a cause rather than a consequence of MASH onset remains very limited. Future studies need to systematically investigate PC morphological changes and their direct impact on hepatocyte lipid metabolism and inflammatory signaling pathways, specifically in MASH animal models or patient samples, to clarify their precise role in the MASH liver-gut-brain axis.

Multi-Axis Metabolic Imbalance in MASH Pathogenesis
A growing body of recent research recognizes the association between the “gut-liver axis” and MASH,[35] yet therapeutic breakthroughs remain scarce. We therefore summarize a more comprehensive framework of organ axes, including the “gut-liver-microbiota axis,” the horizontal gut-liver-pancreas axis, and the vertical brain-gut-liver axis. This will serve as contextual background for subsequent discussion on leveraging PCs for MASH treatment.

Dysregulation of the Gut-Liver-Microbiota Axis
Microbial abundance, metabolites, and gut permeability play crucial roles in MASH development. Studies show that the gut microbiota of MASH patients has significantly higher abundances of Proteobacteria and Fusobacteria compared to healthy individuals.[36] Microbial metabolites also critically influence MASH. The gut microbiota converts primary bile acids (BAs, e.g., CA and CDCA) into secondary BAs, thereby activating the farnesoid X receptor (FXR) and the membrane receptor TGR5.[37] However, downregulated FXR expression in MASH patients leads to uncontrolled BA synthesis and exacerbates hepatic inflammation.[38] Furthermore, increased intestinal permeability allows harmful substances like endotoxins to reach the liver, activating immune responses and ultimately triggering hepatic inflammation.[39] These three factors interact and collectively contribute to MASH pathology, information vital for its treatment.

Dysfunction of the Liver-Gut-Pancreas Axis as a Metabolic Axis
Metabolic aspects of the liver-gut-pancreas axis relate to glucose and lipid homeostasis, reflected in increased risks of human comorbidities. MASH can induce IR, impairing insulin action (e.g., through reduced insulin receptor expression, ineffective receptor binding, or impaired insulin signaling).[40] Insulin regulates neuronal development and can induce neurodegeneration in the central nervous system (CNS) through signaling pathways such as the phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K) and mitogen-activated protein kinase pathways, suggesting a bottom-up influence from MASH. Epidemiological studies indicate that MASH patients are at greater risk for type 2 diabetes (T2D).[41] The “twin-cycle” hypothesis proposes that fat accumulation in the liver and pancreas exacerbates IR, impairs pancreatic regulation of glucose homeostasis, and ultimately leads to T2D.[42] T2D significantly increases the risk of MASH in obese adults and accelerates progression from MASH to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and even HCC.[43] Related mechanisms primarily involve glucose and lipid metabolism (including glucotoxicity and lipotoxicity[44]), IR (increased lipolysis, FFA delivery to the liver, hepatic fatty acid β-oxidation causing oxidative stress[45]), and alterations in insulin secretion.

Dysfunction of the Brain-Gut-Liver Axis as a Neural Axis
The brain-gut-liver axis connects the CNS with gut microbiota, the enteric nervous system, and the neuroendocrine system, participating in the vertical systemic effects of MASH in the body. Direct evidence links MASH to brain function: Within the bidirectional regulatory mechanism of the vagus nerve, intrahepatic vagal afferent fibers sense lipid metabolism signals and provide feedback through the brainstem nucleus tractus solitarius to regulate hepatic very-low-density lipoprotein secretion; the CNS (e.g., hypothalamus) inhibits hepatic lipid synthesis through the leptin-vagal axis, a pathway often characterized by leptin resistance in MASH patients.[46] Chronic MASH leading to varying degrees of liver fibrosis can cause white matter lesions, thereby reducing cognitive function. Concurrently, in this chronic inflammatory state, reduced vagal tone further amplifies intrahepatic inflammatory responses.[47] In the gut, microbial metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) directly regulate sympathetic nervous system activity through G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR)41,[48] which can promote microglial overactivation, leading to neuronal damage.[49]

PC: A Metabolic Hub for Cross-System Regulation in MASH
Within the liver, PCs prominently protrude from the apical surface of cholangiocytes, being present in BECs (BECs, also called cholangiocytes). PCs are also found on quiescent HSCs, where they disassemble during HSC activation and hepatic fibrogenesis.[50] Notably, a key mechanism in liver fibrosis is HSC activation. Although biopsy evidence for PCs on hepatocytes is currently lacking, this does not preclude the potential role of the PC as a metabolic hub regulating MASH pathological progression. Viewing MASH through the lens of the PC links it to metabolic syndrome, highlighting its therapeutic potential.

Before a detailed discussion, we first provide a succinct summary of how alterations in PC parameters (e.g., changes in length, functional gain or loss) within various organs discussed herein influence MASH progression, as detailed in Table 1.

PC and the Liver-Gut-Pancreas Axis: Regulation of the Energy Metabolism Axis
Within the gut-liver-pancreas axis, PC-mediated regulation of insulin secretion in β-cells (through GLP-1/FFAR4/GPCR signaling) and HSC activation are mechanisms most directly linked to MASH fibrosis.

In the pancreas, PCs exhibit motility,[57] enabling them to more effectively sense dynamic changes in microenvironmental metabolites like glucose. Axon-cilium synapses form between β-cell cilia and cholinergic islet innervation.[58] Internally, this allows real-time regulation of insulin secretion; externally, it facilitates signal transmission and linkage. This precise regulation depends, at least partly, on the enriched GPCR signaling platform on cilia, including the GLP-1 receptor sensing the gut hormone glucagon-like peptide-1 and FFAR4 sensing long-chain fatty acids.[59,60] PC function is also crucial for overall pancreatic development and homeostasis. Expression of the intraflagellar transport protein gene Ift88 in pancreatic ducts and islets, whose loss causes ciliary assembly defects, leads to exocrine tissue cyst formation, acinar cell apoptosis, and pancreatic atrophy.[61] Arrest or loss of PC formation is a hallmark across stages of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, underscoring the necessity of PCs for normal pancreatic structure and function. Evidence indicates that PC structural abnormalities impair β-cell paracrine signaling and insulin secretion, ultimately correlating with diabetes development.[59,62] This review aims to explore and connect how PCs influence various stages of MASH; in this context, we posit this step as the initiating event in energy metabolism axis dysregulation.

We propose that dysregulation of PC signaling at the pancreatic end triggers a cascade of reactions throughout the liver-gut-pancreas axis, driving MASH progression. Impaired PC signaling in β-cells disrupts the timing and quantity of insulin secretion, inducing IR. PCs are key nodes integrating downstream PI3K/ protein kinase B (Akt)/mTOR signaling from leptin and insulin; their absence or dysfunction disrupts this pathway, exacerbating both leptin and IR.[62] The resulting systemic metabolic disturbances – elevated free fatty acids and blood glucose – persistently burden the liver. Within the liver, metabolic stresses such as lipotoxicity and ER stress, along with the ensuing inflammatory state, impair PC function in hepatocytes and HSCs.[63] PC damage not only weakens cellular homeostasis maintenance (e.g., by affecting autophagic flux to exacerbate cellular stress[64–67]) but, more importantly, may release normal inhibition on pro-fibrogenic pathways such as Hedgehog (Hh) and Wnt.[68,69] Quiescent HSCs are abnormally activated, transforming into myofibroblasts that produce excessive extracellular matrix (ECM), becoming central to fibrosis progression. At the intestinal end of the axis, the abundant PCs in lamina propria fibroblasts decrease in number and exhibit structural defects under inflammatory conditions,[70,71] potentially disrupting the balance of local tissue repair and immune regulation. Abnormal signals from these cells may further impact the liver through the portal system, collectively exacerbating MASH pathology.

Functional loss of PCs within the liver-gut-pancreas axis, as a systemic regulatory network, leads to glucose and lipid metabolism dysregulation. Combined with aberrant signals of intestinal origin, this creates a microenvironment that damages hepatic PC function and promotes HSC activation and fibrosis, thereby driving the irreversible progression from simple steatosis to MASH and fibrosis.

PC and the Liver-Gut-Brain Axis: Integrative Regulation of the Neuro-Metabolic Axis
PCs are present on neurons, where they control neurite growth and development[72] and process energy metabolism signals.[73] Hypothalamic PCs, in particular, regulate feeding behavior, acting as “central sensors” for energy homeostasis. PCs on pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) and neuropeptide Y (NPY) neurons in the arcuate nucleus (ARC) are especially crucial. Evidence shows that disrupting these cilia (e.g., by knocking out IFT88 or KIF3A) impairs POMC neuron function, leading to adult-onset obesity,[51,74] establishing a causal link between ciliogenesis and body weight regulation. Moreover, central PCs modulate sensitivity to hormones including leptin and insulin.[75] The melanocortin 4 receptor (MC4R) pathway, localized to PCs, plays a central role.[76] POMC neurons release α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone, activating MC4R to suppress appetite;[77] similarly, defective MC4R gene expression can cause obesity.[78]

Thus, the hypothalamic-PC-MC4R axis can be viewed as a high-weight pathway in cilia-related appetite regulation, tightly coupled to leptin signaling. Leptin primarily acts on AgRP and POMC neurons in the ARC, suppressing appetite by activating POMC neurons. The leptin resistance common in obesity may form a vicious cycle with PC defects. For instance, the average length and surface area of hypothalamic cilia are significantly reduced (by over 40%) in obese mice,[79] a shortening phenotype likely both a consequence and an exacerbating factor of impaired signal transduction.

Extending this view to the liver-gut-brain axis, PCs constitute a systemic regulatory network. In the liver, PCs on HSCs and BECs regulate cell activation and proliferation through pathways like Hh, Wnt, and Notch, influencing fibrosis. Modulating Notch signaling can reduce fibrotic deposition.[80] Genetic (e.g., PKD2 mutation) or acquired (inflammatory cytokines, ER stress) damage can impair ciliary function, causing intracellular Ca2+/cAMP signaling imbalance.[81] This triggers VEGF-driven angiogenesis and HSC activation[25] as well as β-catenin-mediated chemokine (e.g., CXCL10) secretion, recruiting macrophages and promoting inflammation and fibrosis.[26] These processes align with the ductular reaction and periportal fibrosis observed in MASH. We hypothesize that dysfunctional PC in intrahepatic cholangiocytes may integrate metabolic stress signals and translate them into VEGF-mediated angiogenesis and β-catenin/chemokine-mediated inflammatory-fibrotic responses, thereby driving progression from simple steatosis to MASH and fibrosis. In the CNS, PCs regulate hormonal activity. Impaired cilia may affect lipid metabolism, worsening MASH. Furthermore, PCs have been confirmed in some subtypes of glial cells and interstitial cells of Cajal within the enteric nervous system.[82] Studies also show that the gut microbiota regulates numerous host metabolic processes, including energy homeostasis, glucose metabolism, and lipid metabolism[83,84] and is even linked to brain regions processing sensory information.[85] This relationship is bidirectional: Brain-derived signals can top-down alter gut microbiota composition, and microbial metabolites can influence human brain structure.

We propose the following hypothesis: Hypothalamic PC dysfunction leading to feeding dysregulation and systemic metabolic disturbances will exacerbate hepatic lipid accumulation and inflammation through circulatory factors (e.g., bile acids, metabolites) or neural signals. Conversely, MASH-associated systemic inflammation and metabolic disturbances may also damage cilia in the hypothalamus and other brain regions, where microglial activation-mediated neuroinflammation is considered a key node linking peripheral metabolic disorder to central ciliopathy and cognitive decline.

Although the local functions of PCs in individual organs are being revealed, the integrated picture of how they synergistically drive MASH progression at the multi-organ axis level remains unclear. We propose an integrative hypothesis: Under genetic predisposition or high-fat diet induction, functional loss or shortening of the hypothalamic PC-MC4R signal is an early event in central regulatory failure, leading to hyperphagia and obesity. The ensuing hyperleptinemia, IR, and gut microbiota dysbiosis collectively create a microenvironment that damages PCs in hepatocytes and hepatic non-parenchymal cells, accelerating hepatic steatosis and inflammation. Simultaneously, peripheral inflammatory signals ascend to the brain, potentially damaging neuronal PC function by activating microglia, forming a vicious cycle that drives progression from simple steatosis to MASH and even extrahepatic complications. Future research should employ causal interventions at the axis level in MASH animal models and quantitatively assess the precise effect size of such interventions on core MASH phenotypes such as hepatic fat content, inflammation score, and fibrosis degree, to validate this hypothesis and elucidate core mechanisms.

Therapeutic Implications of PC-Associated Pathways in MASH
Based on the central role of PCs in MASH pathogenesis, interventions targeting their associated signaling pathways have emerged as a highly promising therapeutic strategy. Restoring or modulating PC function and the key pathways they mediate holds potential to intervene in disease progression across multiple layers, including lipid metabolism, inflammatory responses, fibrogenesis, and neuro-immune regulation. The following sections elaborate on the therapeutic significance of PC-linked pathways – mTOR, Hh, Wnt/β-catenin, Notch, transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β)/Smad, and sympathetic/vagal nerve regulation – in MASH, exploring potential drug intervention directions based on these pathways (Fig. 1).

To further advance the clinical translation of this strategy, future efforts should focus on constructing a PC-based biomarker system (e.g., ciliary-associated proteins, specific imaging features) to enable precise identification and dynamic monitoring of disease status. Concurrently, identifying advantaged patient subgroups likely to benefit from cilia-targeted therapies is crucial. Such subgroups may include obese patients with T2D exhibiting advanced liver fibrosis and severe IR, or patients with metabolic-associated neurocognitive impairment. Implementing precision interventions for these key populations holds promise for breaking the current therapeutic bottleneck and achieving effective translation from mechanistic insight to clinical benefit.

mTOR Signaling Pathway
Liver kinase B1 protein, located within the PC, negatively regulates the mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1), serving as a key molecular link between PC mechanosensation and mTOR signaling.[86] mTORC1 activity correlates with PC length, with enhanced activity increasing ciliary length.[87] Within the mTOR pathway, mTORC1 is a downstream effector of PI3K/AKT signaling. Following PI3K/AKT activation, phosphorylation and inhibition of the Tuberous Sclerosis Complex 2 (TSC2) relieves its suppression of Rheb, thereby activating mTORC1.[88] Activated mTORC1 promotes lipid synthesis through sterol regulatory element-binding protein (SREBP) transcription factors, fostering hepatic steatosis. Upstream, IR-associated hyperinsulinemia activates the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, leading to lipid accumulation through the above process.[88,89] Concurrently, multiple pathological processes synergistically drive MASH initiation and progression, including oxidative stress[90] and chronic inflammation.[91] During oxidative stress, accumulated hepatic ROS can oxidatively modify the critical Cys124 residue of phosphatase and tensin homolog, inactivating it and thereby removing its negative regulation on PI3K/Akt. This further contributes to persistent aberrant activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway. Chronic inflammation and hepatocyte injury activate HSCs, promoting fibrosis. Pro-fibrogenic factors like TGF-β secreted by HSCs continuously stimulate the PI3K/AKT pathway.[92] Collectively, these processes make the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway an engine driving progression from MASH to fibrosis and HCC.

Hh Signaling Pathway
Evc and Evc2 are transmembrane proteins that interact at the PC base; their knockout or defective expression attenuates Hh signaling.[93] TMEM216, a transmembrane protein at the ciliary base, also weakens Hh signaling when deficient.[94] Normally quiescent in the liver, the Hh pathway activates upon injury to facilitate regeneration. However, persistent liver damage leads to prolonged Hh signaling.[95] Hepatocytes continuously produce Hh ligands, causing aberrant pathway activation.[96] Overactivation upregulates the long non-coding RNA Hilnc through the downstream transcription factor Gli. Highly expressed Hilnc specifically binds the RNA-binding protein IGF2BP2 in the cytoplasm, stabilizing peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ), leading to elevated hepatic PPARγ protein levels and promoting lipogenesis.[96] Concurrently, Hh ligands released from damaged hepatocytes act in a paracrine manner on HSCs, activating their internal Hh pathway, evidenced by nuclear translocation of Gli proteins and target gene expression. Hh-Gli activation drives expression of pro-inflammatory factors (e.g., TNF-α, interleukin-6), exacerbating inflammation and injury, even promoting ballooning,[97] and fosters HSC activation and fibrogenic progression, thereby aggravating MASH.

Wnt/β-Catenin Signaling Pathway
The kinesin KIF3a participates in ciliary assembly, maintenance and regulates Wnt/β-catenin signaling.[98] Inversin acts as a molecular switch for Wnt signaling, forming a protein complex with Dishevelled.[99] A specific Inversin compartment exists within the PC; its absence does not affect PC structure but disrupts the establishment of polarized duct systems in the liver and pancreas.[100] Hyperglycemia drives intestinal barrier dysfunction and risk for enteric infection.[101] It can also activate the intestinal Wnt/β-catenin pathway. Moreover, restraint stress similarly disrupts intestinal homeostasis;[102] in this context, compensatory activation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway can protect the gut-vascular barrier and delay NASH progression.[103] In the liver, liver-specific β-catenin knockout mice exhibit defects in bile acid and cholesterol homeostasis and increased susceptibility to metabolism-driven steatohepatitis.[104] Overactivation of the hepatic Wnt/β-catenin pathway upregulates lipogenic genes (e.g., SREBP-1c) and suppresses fatty acid oxidation genes (e.g., PPARα), collectively promoting hepatic lipogenesis.[105] Furthermore, excessive pathway activation suppresses PPARγ transcriptional activity through regulators such as necdin and DLK1. Decreased PPARγ expression promotes HSC proliferation, activation, and fibrosis.[106]

Notch Signaling Pathway
Notch receptors are located on the PC membrane, while Presenilin-2, the enzyme that cleaves and activates Notch, resides at the ciliary basal body. This spatial proximity provides a structural basis for localized Notch signal activation.[107] Aberrant Notch activation inhibits PC formation, shortening cilia and suppressing function.[108] Activated Notch signaling, through its intracellular domain (NICD), promotes expression of the transcription factor Sox9, which upregulates osteopontin.[109] Osteopontin, a key fibrogenic factor, directly drives HSC activation and promotes liver fibrogenesis.[109] This pathway’s abnormal activation stems from increased expression of the upstream ligand Jagged1 (JAG1), a process driven by gut microbiota dysbiosis through the hepatocyte Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)-nuclear factor kappa (NF-κB) signaling axis.[110] Human liver biopsies and mouse NASH models show positive correlations between hepatic JAG1 expression and disease activity scores, fibrosis stage, and Notch target gene (HES1, HEYL) levels. Hepatocyte-specific Jag1 knockout protects mice from NASH-induced fibrosis.[111]

TGF-β/Smad Signaling Pathway
In the pancreas, PC deficiency (e.g., Kif3a, Ift88, or Cby1 knockout) leads to ciliary loss in pancreatic ductal cells, upregulates TGF-β1 expression, and activates downstream Smad3 signaling. This promotes pancreatic stellate cell activation and excessive ECM deposition, ultimately causing pancreatic inflammation, fibrosis, and acinar cell atrophy.[112] The PC membrane harbors TGF-β receptors. Upon ligand binding, activated receptors migrate from the ciliary membrane to the ciliary pocket and enter the cell through clathrin-mediated endocytosis. This process is crucial for activating downstream SMAD transcription factors (e.g., SMAD2/3), which then translocate to the nucleus to regulate target gene transcription.[113] In MASH, damaged hepatocytes and inflammatory cells release TGF-β1. Binding to receptors on HSCs activates downstream Smad2/3 phosphorylation. The resulting Smad complex translocates to the nucleus, promoting excessive ECM deposition.[114] In addition, TGF-β1 induces epithelial-mesenchymal transition in hepatic oval cells, converting them to HSCs and aggravating fibrosis.[115]

Sympathetic Nervous System Regulatory Pathway
In the nervous system, most neurons possess a single PC, which has been shown to be crucial for maintaining excitatory-inhibitory balance in neural circuits.[73] Animal studies indicate that PC loss or dysfunction in the ventromedial hypothalamus reduces sympathetic nerve tone and causes central leptin resistance, lowering energy expenditure and leading to obesity,[116] a high-risk factor for MASH. Investigations using three-dimensional (3D) immunoimaging to explore liver innervation integrity across NAFLD stages revealed degenerative features in sympathetic nerves, including collapsed dendritic arborization, with degeneration severity correlating with NAFLD pathology.[117] This results from chronic sympathetic over-excitation.[118] In this context, reducing aberrant hepatic sympathetic nerve activation can effectively counteract liver steatosis.[119] Therefore, both sympathetic suppression and chronic over-excitation are MASH risk factors, and intact PC structure likely exerts a positive influence on neuronal electrical activity.

Vagus Nerve System Regulatory Pathway
Muscarinic acetylcholine receptor 3 (mAChR M3) is present in the PCs of cerebrovascular cells,[120] a key target of the vagus nerve. Activating mAChR M3 enhances ciliary length[121] and delays MASH progression.[122] Hepatic macrophages, particularly Kupffer cells, are major immune players in MASH. Some studies indicate that reducing Kupffer cells by inhibiting inflammatory pathways (e.g., NF-κB) improves hepatic IR and alleviates MASH.[123] From a vagal perspective, research shows that vagus nerve stimulation activates the α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (α7nAChR), which directly suppresses inflammation through cholinergic signaling and indirectly modulates the unfolded protein response (UPR) pathway in Kupffer cells to inhibit ER stress.[124] This suppresses three UPR arms: PERK/eIF2-α, ATF6, and IRE1/TRAF2/IKK,[125] thereby inhibiting inflammation. Activating α7nAChR inhibits hepatic necroptosis and alleviates acute liver injury,[126] suggesting a potential to delay MASH progression. Furthermore, the vagus nerve establishes streamlined direct connections between the brainstem and gut,[127] also influencing MASH progression.

Potential MASH Therapeutics Based on PC Pathways
At present, no MASH therapeutics explicitly developed based on PCs exist. However, potential links to PCs can be found among known preclinical or clinical drugs. For instance, Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6) mediates autophagy-dependent PC disassembly. HDAC6 overexpression in cholangiocarcinoma reduces PC expression and promotes tumor growth, while HDAC6 inhibition restores cilia, which may slow disease progression. The HDAC6 inhibitor ricolinostat inhibits cholangiocarcinoma cell proliferation, an effect enhanced when combined with ciliogenesis-promoting agents like the SCFAs butyrate.[128,129] Other studies show Ricolinostat can delay renal fibrosis through the TGF-β pathway.[130] This evidence suggests Ricolinostat might exert anti-fibrotic effects in MASH through PC-related mechanisms. Therefore, we posit that adding PC-restoring agents to conventional MASH treatment strategies could yield superior clinical efficacy, ideally through more precise selection based on specific PC pathways. It is also worth noting that lipid-based nanoparticles possess high liver-targeting efficiency, stability, and safety.[130] Their co-administration with relevant drugs (e.g., SB431542-Loaded Liposomes, as shown in the following tables)[131] may further improve therapeutic outcomes.

Tables 2 and 3 list drugs validated in clinical trials or animal studies to improve hepatic pathology and illustrate their relationship to PC pathways.

Limitations and Future Directions
While targeting PC offers a novel therapeutic avenue for MASH, significant limitations remain. The foremost bottleneck is the lack of longitudinal human data on PCs in the MASH context, primarily due to technical challenges in achieving high-resolution, high-throughput detection of PCs in clinical samples (especially paraffin-embedded tissues), making dynamic assessment of their signaling activity difficult. Furthermore, PC-associated signaling pathways exhibit considerable crosstalk, posing a risk of off-target effects during intervention. However, advances in detection technologies, such as novel elastography methods including ultrasound-based acoustic radiation force impulse imaging, can already assess liver fibrosis in ciliopathy patients. Future, more sensitive PC detection methods hold promise for revealing associations between different ciliary gene variants and fibrosis risk, and for identifying MASH subgroups more responsive to PC-targeted therapy.[143] Therefore, PCs may serve not only as therapeutic targets but also as biological indicators for disease monitoring and prognosis.

Conclusion
Regarding drug development, future efforts should focus on screening or designing compounds that can specifically modulate PC assembly, length, or signal transduction, based on known PC pathways, followed by systematic functional validation in MASH models. Studies should incorporate dynamic monitoring of PC-related biomarkers (e.g., ciliary structural proteins, signaling activity molecules) to clarify the correlation between drug efficacy and PC status. This would provide more compelling preclinical evidence for PC-targeted MASH therapy. Integrating cross-technology, cross-model research has the potential to gradually overcome current limitations and advance PC-targeted strategies from mechanistic exploration towards clinical translation.

paper.title: A review on gedunin as an anticancer agent: molecular mechanisms, preclinical evidence, and translational challenges.
paper.journal: Phytomedicine : international journal of phytotherapy and phytopharmacology
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Gedunin is a limonoid natural product that has demonstrated anticancer activity in preclinical experimental models. However, findings vary across cancer types and experimental systems, and the extent to which its proposed molecular targets have been validated remains uncertain.

OBJECTIVE: This systematic review evaluated the preclinical anticancer effects of gedunin, focusing on its reported molecular targets and signaling pathways, effects on cancer stem-cell phenotypes and chemoresistance, formulation and combination strategies, and translational limitations.

METHODS: The review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar were searched from database inception to July 2026. Eligible studies were original, peer-reviewed investigations of chemically identified gedunin in in vitro, in vivo, or cancer-related mechanistic and biochemical models. Reviews, conference abstracts, preprints, studies of crude plant extracts without chemically identified gedunin, duplicate publications, and studies without relevant pharmacological or mechanistic outcomes were excluded. Data on cancer models, experimental conditions, gedunin concentrations or doses, molecular findings, pharmacological outcomes, and translational relevance were extracted. Because of differences in cancer models, experimental designs, and outcome measures, findings were synthesized narratively rather than quantitatively.

RESULTS: The search identified 1048 records. Following removal of 877 duplicates, 171 records were screened by title and abstract, and 149 were excluded. Twenty-two full-text reports were assessed, of which four were excluded, leaving 18 independent original studies. Gedunin was reported to exert antiproliferative, pro-apoptotic, cell-cycle-modulating, anti-invasive, anti-stemness, and chemosensitizing effects across several experimental cancer models. Reported molecular associations involved heat shock protein 90 (HSP90)-related proteostasis, phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K/AKT), Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK/STAT), nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB), mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), Sonic Hedgehog/Glioma-associated oncogene (Shh/Gli), focal adhesion kinase/Rho-associated coiled-coil-containing protein kinase (FAK/ROCK), oxidative-stress responses, and mitochondrial apoptotic signaling. Selected studies also reported activity against cancer stem-cell-associated phenotypes and drug-resistant models, while nanoformulation and combination approaches enhanced activity in experimental systems. Evidence for a direct interaction between gedunin and prostaglandin E synthase 3 (p23) was primarily derived from one study and remains insufficiently replicated. Overall, the evidence was dominated by in vitro investigations, with limited characterization of pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, systematic toxicity, and efficacy in clinically relevant in vivo models.

CONCLUSION: Current evidence supports gedunin as a promising preclinical anticancer candidate, but not as a clinically validated anticancer agent or a compound with definitively validated molecular targets. The p23-HSP90 axis represents a candidate mechanism requiring independent confirmation through genetic perturbation, rescue experiments, direct target-engagement assays such as cellular thermal shift assays (CETSA), and biophysical approaches including surface plasmon resonance (SPR) or isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). Future studies should prioritize standardized gedunin preparations, rigorous target validation, pharmacokinetic and biodistribution characterization, optimized delivery systems, systematic toxicological evaluation, biomarker-guided combination strategies, and validation in clinically relevant in vivo models. At present, safety evidence should be regarded as limited preclinical data; systematic toxicology remains unknown.

paper.title: The RARγ antagonist CD2665 attenuates ATRA-induced growth plate impairment by preserving chondrocyte homeostasis.
paper.abstract: All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA)-based therapy is clinically important but may cause skeletal toxicity during development. The contribution of retinoic acid receptor γ (RARγ) to ATRA-associated growth plate injury remains unclear. This study investigated whether the RARγ antagonist CD2665 attenuates ATRA-induced growth plate impairment and whether it compromises ATRA-induced responses in HL-60 cells. Juvenile Sprague-Dawley rats were treated with vehicle, ATRA, ATRA plus CD2665, or CD2665. Skeletal growth, growth plate morphology, RAR subtype expression, chondrocyte fate-related markers, apoptosis-related proteins, and IHH-GLI1 protein expression were assessed. Primary growth plate chondrocytes were used to evaluate viability, proliferation, apoptosis, cell-cycle distribution, and related proteins, while HL-60 cells were used to assess ATRA-induced growth inhibition and myeloid differentiation. ATRA selectively decreased RARγ immunoreactivity among RAR subtypes in the growth plate, reduced skeletal growth and growth plate height, altered growth plate zonal architecture, and decreased IHH and GLI1 protein expression in tissues and primary chondrocytes. CD2665 partially attenuated these abnormalities and improved selected chondrocyte fate-related markers. CD2665 also reduced ATRA-associated Annexin V positivity in primary chondrocytes, although its effects on BAX and BCL-2 were limited. In HL-60 cells, CD2665 did not compromise ATRA-induced growth inhibition, G0/G1-phase accumulation, maturation-associated morphology, or CD11b/CD14 upregulation. These findings indicate that CD2665 partially attenuates ATRA-induced growth retardation and growth plate impairment, in association with preservation of IHH and GLI1 protein expression and partial improvement of chondrocyte fate-related changes, without obvious compromise of ATRA-induced differentiation-associated responses in HL-60 cells under the present experimental conditions.

paper.title: Hexafluoropropylene oxide dimer acid disrupts intestinal health and gut microbial networks of the native earthworm Metaphire guillelmi in agricultural soil.
paper.abstract: Hexafluoropropylene oxide dimer acid (HFPO-DA), a short-chain PFAS alternative to perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), is increasingly detected in agricultural soils, but ecologically relevant indicators of its toxicity to native soil invertebrates remain insufficiently defined. Here, using wheat-field soil as a realistic exposure medium, we exposed Metaphire guillelmi to HFPO-DA (0.02 and 0.2 mg kg-1) for 28 days and included PFOA at equivalent doses as a benchmark. We integrated oxidative stress biomarkers, digestive enzyme activity, the 8-hydroxy-2-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG), histopathology, integrated biomarker response version 2 (IBRv2), transcriptomics, 16S rRNA sequencing, LEfSe, and microbial network analyses to establish a multi-level indicator framework for assessing the risks associated with PFAS alternatives. HFPO-DA yielded a lower relative IBRv2 value than PFOA at 0.2 mg kg-1 after 28 days, yet it generated specific adverse effects, including elevated DNA damage and visible intestinal epithelial injury even at 0.02 mg kg-1. Transcriptomic analyses revealed concentration-specific changes in genes associated with fatty acid metabolism and PPAR signaling at the low dose, and with oxidative phosphorylation, neurotransmitter-related pathways, and Hedgehog signaling at the high dose. Gut microbial analyses further showed that 0.2 mg kg-1 HFPO-DA reduced α-diversity, altered the relative abundances of bacterial taxa, and simplified co-occurrence networks. Collectively, these results indicate that HFPO-DA can impair intestinal health, alter gut microbial communities, and induce transcriptional changes in a native earthworm. Our findings support using integrated host-microbiome indicators as early-warning tools to evaluate hidden ecological risks associated with emerging PFAS alternatives in agricultural soils.

paper.title: Stepwise Derivation and Characterization of Midbrain Dopamine Neurons from Human Pluripotent Stem Cells.
paper.abstract: Human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived midbrain dopamine (mDA) neurons have become an important and scalable cell source for Parkinson's disease (PD) modeling, drug discovery, and cell replacement therapy. Reliable generation of mDA neurons from hPSCs require precise control and quality assessment of floor plate induction, neurogenic conversion, and neuronal maturation throughout differentiation. The WNT-Boost strategy improves midbrain patterning through biphasic WNT activation and is currently being evaluated in clinical studies. The WNT-Boost+ approach further modifies the WNT-Boost protocol during neurogenic conversion to improve the yield and subtype identity of mDA neurons. Here, we describe a detailed WNT-Boost+ differentiation protocol for generating and validating hPSC-derived mDA neurons. The protocol incorporates high-density single-cell seeding, dual-SMAD inhibition, Sonic Hedgehog (SHH)-mediated ventral floor plate induction, stage-specific WNT modulation, optimized neurogenic conversion, sequential replating, and neuronal maturation under defined culture conditions. Critical stage-specific quality controls include mRNA gene expression analysis, immunocytochemical characterization, and post-thaw recovery assessment. The successfully differentiated cultures showed greater than 80% FOXA2+ expression on Day 16 and greater than 40% FOXA2+TH+ expression on Day 40, and cryopreserved Day 16 progenitors retained more than 80% viability and FOXA2 expression after thawing. This stepwise workflow enables robust and reproducible generation of mDA neurons and provides a practical framework for PD modeling-based mechanistic studies and translational applications.

paper.title: Machine Learning Based Plasma Proteomic Analysis Identifies Disease Differentiating Biomarkers in Atopic Dermatitis.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Inflammatory diseases consist of a diverse group of conditions characterized by immune responses leading to inflammation causing damage and abnormality in function. Atopic dermatitis (AD) and ulcerative colitis (UC) both exhibit aberrant Th2 cell activity, leading to epithelial barrier dysfunction in the skin and gut, respectively. Although both diseases share similar features, differences in their tissue-specific pathology, clinical manifestations, and immune profiles may provide valuable insights into the distinct mechanisms underlying each disease.

METHODS: We used the high-throughput Olink 384 proximity extension assay platform to profile plasma proteins from 58 patients with AD or UC and 29 healthy subjects. Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were identified and machine-learning (ML) model using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was conducted to select disease-differentiating biomarkers. Pearson correlation analysis was performed to identify protein modules associated with severity of AD.

RESULTS: DEP analysis yielded 85 (35 unique) and 99 (49 unique) upregulated proteins in AD and UC, respectively, compared to healthy subjects. We integrated an ML model and selected 24 proteins to distinguish between the diseases, which accurately predicted disease-differentiating biomarkers based on distinctive proteomic signatures and disease severity. Using nested cross-validation approach, we achieved robust classification performance with a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.99 ± 0.01. Correlation analysis with disease severity identified upregulated ML-selected proteins such as CCL13, CCL26, CD70, CDON, LY6D and MMP1 in AD, and ITM2A and REG4 in UC. Among these identified proteins, we suggest CDON, CD70, and LY6D, which had highly correlated expression levels, as AD-specific biomarkers.

CONCLUSION: Our study provides insight into the application of ML algorithms for disease diagnosis, and our model may be expanded to other disease contexts. Our results identify inflammatory protein biomarkers and suggest their relevance in predicting disease severity, monitoring clinical progression and future therapeutic strategies.
paper.full_text:
INTRODUCTION
Inflammatory diseases consist of a diverse group of conditions characterized by immune responses leading to inflammation causing damage and abnormality in function. Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic inflammatory skin condition, affecting about 2% to 10% of adults and 10% to 30% of pediatric patients in developed nations.1 Patients with AD experience heightened activity of T helper (Th) cells, especially Th2 subtype, which lead to inflammation and cause skin barrier dysfunction.23 On the other hand, ulcerative colitis (UC) is an idiopathic inflammatory gut condition with an incidence rate ranging from 9 to 20 cases per 100,000 individuals annually.45 In the case of UC, similar to AD, there exists an aberrant Th2 cell response, consequently resulting in impairment of the gut epithelial barrier.67 Although AD and UC share features of epithelial barrier dysfunction and systemic immune dysregulation, differences in their tissue-specific pathology, clinical manifestations and immune profiles may provide valuable insights into the distinct mechanisms underlying each disease.

Proteomic profiling of inflammatory diseases has been widely used, aiming to define disease-specific biomarkers. Nevertheless, traditional data analysis methods face constraints when dealing with large databases.8 Conventional statistical techniques interpret data using pre-established models and hypotheses, frequently assuming specific distributions. Focusing on inference and parameter estimation could be less effective with complex, high dimensional datasets. Consequently, the application of machine learning (ML) methods for data analysis emerges as crucial and offers a promising way to discover the intricate biomarker signatures and immunopathogenic mechanisms associated with inflammatory diseases.910 While ML can handle large-scale datasets, its key strength lies in its ability to regularize models, prevent overfitting, and ensure better generalization to new data, enhancing our comprehension of these complex diseases using proteomic profiling.

In this study, to identify disease-differentiating biomarkers for AD and UC, we conducted proteomic profiling of 363 proteins in plasma of 58 patients with moderate to severe AD or UC, and 29 healthy individuals using the Olink proximity extension assay Inflammation I panel. We also integrated proteomic expression profiling with ML based approaches using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression to select protein set modules that can be used to classify signature markers of each inflammatory disease.

Patient recruitment and inclusion
Plasma samples from patients and healthy donors of Korean ethnicity were collected at Seoul National University Hospital. In healthy control (HC) group, subjects with atopic and inflammatory comorbidities such as AD, inflammatory bowel disease, allergic rhinitis, asthma, or allergic conjunctivitis were excluded. AD patients were stratified into three disease severity groups as measured by eczema area and severity index (EASI) scores, mild: EASI < 16, moderate: 16 ≤ EASI < 23, and severe: EASI ≥ 23.11 Disease activity of UC patients was assessed using Mayo score, which consists of four components including stool frequency, rectal bleeding, endoscopic findings and physical global assessment. The total score is between 0 and 12, with each part getting a score from 0 to 3. Based on these criteria, a total score of 3–5 indicates mild, 6–10 indicates moderate and 11–12 indicates severe disease activity.12

All enrolled participants (n = 87) were included in DEP analysis and ML analysis (Fig. 1). For severity correlation analysis, exclusions were applied due to incomplete or clinically non-representative severity data. Among the AD patients, one lacked a recorded EASI score and three had EASI scores below 10, consistent with mild disease status, and were therefore excluded. Similarly, four UC patients were not examined or only partial score was available, and were therefore excluded from the analysis.

Details about patient information and clinical characteristics can be found in Table 1. For treatment-related analyses, patients were included if drug initiation occurred prior to blood collection based on known pharmacokinetic half-life. Patients with no treatment records (AD: n = 2; UC: n = 2) or those who initiated treatment on the same day as blood collection (AD: n = 21; UC: n = 9) were excluded from drug-effect analysis (Supplementary Fig. 1).

Sample collection and proteomic profiling
All blood was obtained from each donor using heparin Cell Preparation Tubes (cat No. 362753, BD Vacutainer®, Becton Dickinson, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA). Blood processing occurred within two hours (1,800 × g, 20 minutes, room temperature (RT)). Plasma was aliquoted and stored at −80°C until data generation. Proteomics data were generated using Olink 384 inflammation I panel (Uppsala, Sweden) shown in Supplementary Table 1. Quality control was conducted according to the manufacturer’s guidelines, including evaluation of internal incubation, extension, and detection controls. Assay performance was assessed using the coefficient of variation (CV), and proteins with high technical variability (CV > 20%) were excluded from downstream analyses. Detection rate was defined as the proportion of samples with Normalized protein expression (NPX) values above the assay-specific limit of detection (LOD); proteins detected in less than 75% of samples were removed. For values below LOD, NPX values provided by Olink were retained as recommended, as they reflect normalized relative quantification on a log2 scale.

Statistical analysis
DEP analysis was conducted using the Mann-Whitney U test at a confidence level of 0.95. Multiple correction testing was applied using the Benjamini-Hochberg method and proteins with P < 0.01 and |log2 fold change (FC)| ≥ 0.5 were considered disease-associated proteins (Supplementary Fig. 2, Supplementary Tables 2 and 3). Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed using OlinkAnalyze (v4.0.2) without excluding proteins and samples (Supplementary Fig. 3). Pearson correlation analysis of upregulated proteins was performed using Python (v3.11.3) with computed P values in Supplementary Tables 4 and 5. Correlation of protein levels and clinical severity were evaluated using simple regression model in GraphPad Prism 9.5.1 (GraphPad Software Inc., San Diego, CA, USA) (Supplementary Figs. 4 and 5).

ML model
A disease prediction model was developed to identify disease-specific proteins using L1-regularized (LASSO) logistic regression. The study cohort comprised 87 samples. To obtain a robust and unbiased estimate of generalization performance and to mitigate the possibility that results were driven by a single favorable split, we employed a nested 5-fold cross-validation framework with explicit separation of hyperparameter tuning and performance evaluation. Within each outer training split, DEPs were identified using only the inner-training data, and the LASSO logistic regression model was fit while selecting the regularization strength λ via inner 5-fold CV over a log-spaced grid λ ∈ {10−6, 10−5, ..., 1, 10, 102}. The outer loop provided an unbiased evaluation of model generalization across folds. For downstream reporting and biological interpretation of the protein signature, we used one representative outer split; in that split, the inner-loop tuning selected λ = 1, and we therefore fixed λ = 1 for the subsequent downstream analyses on that split for consistency and reproducibility. Proteins with non-zero coefficients were selected as biomarker candidates. Model performance was assessed using macro-averaged F1 score, weighted accuracy, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), reported as mean ± standard deviation (Supplementary Fig. 2). To interpret the contribution of each protein to the classification model, we calculated a feature importance score for each protein based on the absolute model coefficients across three one-vs-rest classifiers, summed and min-max normalized to a 0–100 scale for visualization. The model distinguishing each disease from HC was trained using only the outer loop with λ fixed at 1. All ML analyses were performed using scikit-learn (v1.2.2) in Python 3.10.10.

Ethics statement
This study and all experiment protocols were reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Seoul National University Hospital (IRB No. 2104-212-1215 (AD), 2012-115-1183 (UC), 2108-123-1246 (HC), C-2104-212-1215 (HC)), and all subjects provided written informed consent.

Patient demographics
Plasma samples from 29 HC subjects, 37 AD patients, and 21 UC patients were collected from SNU hospital (Fig. 1). Patient demographics are summarized in Table 1. We performed unbiased hierarchical clustering PCA based on NPX values of all cohorts (Supplementary Fig. 3). Variance showed that HC clustered more tightly separately from disease groups, while patients with AD and UC exhibited more dispersed clustering, potentially reflecting disease heterogeneity.

Differentially expressed protein (DEP) analysis
DEP analysis (P < 0.01 and log2 FC of 0.5) revealed 85 and 99 proteins upregulated in AD and UC, respectively compared to HC (Fig. 2A, Supplementary Tables 2 and 3). As expected, many AD-associated pro-inflammatory cytokines (interleukin [IL]-10, IL-13 and IL-18) and chemokines (CCL13, CCL17, CCL22 and CCL26) were elevated in AD, while UC-associated pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-17A, IL-17C and IL-24) and chemokines (CCL17, CCL28 and CXCL1) were increased in UC (Fig. 2B and C).23131415 Alternatively, only one protein, GAL, was found to be downregulated in AD, while two proteins, CCL26 and RAB6A, were downregulated in UC compared to HC (Fig. 2B and C). Of the elevated DEPs, 50 DEPs were identified to overlap between AD and UC (Fig. 2D).

ML model for disease classification predicts potential biomarker candidates
To identify disease-differentiating proteomes, we applied an ML model using LASSO regression of DEP abundance levels (n = 136) at baseline. During cross-validation in the training cohort, 24 proteins were selected in the final predictive model to be relevant to the disease based on protein abundance levels. Using a nested cross-validation approach, we achieved robust classification performance with a mean AUROC of 0.99 ± 0.01. (Fig. 3A). The mean ROC curve with a 99% confidence interval demonstrated discriminating power and generalizability. The overall performance of the classifier in distinguishing among HC, AD and UC was evaluated. All classes achieved AUC score of > 0.75, class 1 in the best performances as measured with the area under the curve (AUC) for each class (AD-AUC: 0.99 ± 0.00, HC-AUC: 1.00 ± 0.00, UC-AUC: 0.96 ± 0.01) on the train dataset. Additional performance metrics across the outer folds further confirmed model reliability: F1 score of 0.957 ± 0.024, weighted accuracy of 0.956 ± 0.025, macro-averaged AUROC of 0.994 ± 0.008, and macro-averaged AUPRC of 0.988 ± 0.019.

To interpret the contribution of each protein to the classification model, we calculated a feature importance score for each protein based on the LASSO logistic regression coefficients (Fig. 3B). The levels of the 24 selected proteins were visualized across groups. Most of the proteins were elevated in one disease cohort, while some proteins were elevated in both cohorts. LY6D had the highest importance score and its expression was specifically increased in AD. Other proteins were also specifically expressed in one of the disease cohorts, such as CCL13 and IL-32 in AD and MMP1 in UC, but had lower importance scores in the ML classification model. Unsupervised hierarchical clustering of the test set using ML-selected proteins showed clustering of disease-associated protein expression in each sample by disease category, although some overlap among conditions was observed (Fig. 3C). Although there was some variation in protein expression levels across individuals possibly due to disease heterogeneity, CCL13, CCL26, KYNU, IL-32 and LY6D were elevated in AD, while ANGPT1, MMP1, PIK3AP1 and PSMG3 were elevated in UC.

To assess potential confounding effects of drug treatments on the selected protein biomarkers, we conducted post-hoc statistical analyses using the Kruskal-Wallis test (Supplementary Tables 4 and 5). In particular, we conducted a rank-sum test for mesalazine-treated versus untreated individuals in the UC cohort and assessed the expression levels of the 24 proteins used in the ML model across various drug treatment groups within the AD cohort (dupilumab, methotrexate, cyclosporine, and prednisolone). Only one protein, MZB1, displayed a statistically significant difference (P < 0.05) between treatment groups in AD among these comparisons. This implies that drug use is unlikely to account for all of the model’s predictive performance, and that the protein panel reflects disease-related biology rather than drug-induced changes.

CCL13, CCL26, CD70, CDON, LY6D and MMP1 are moderately correlated with severity in patients with moderate-to-severe AD
To identify potential biomarker proteins that are correlated with disease severity and play a role in disease progression, we conducted severity correlation analysis using protein expression levels between mild to severe groups (Supplementary Fig. 4). Among ML-selected proteins, six proteins consistently demonstrated moderate correlations with disease severity. CCL13 had the highest positive correlation, and CCL26, CD70, CDON, LY6D and MMP1 were also positively correlated with AD severity (Fig. 4A). The expression of five proteins, CCL13, CCL26, CD70, CDON and LY6D were significantly elevated in AD compared to HC and UC (Fig. 4B). These proteins were combined to classify individuals with moderate-to-severe AD from HC, achieving an AUC of 1.00 ± 0.00 (Fig. 4C).

REG4 and ITM2A are moderately correlated with severity in patients with moderate-to-severe UC
Similarly, we conducted a severity correlation analysis to assess the relationship between protein levels and severity (Supplementary Fig. 5). Among the proteins analyzed, REG4 exhibited moderate correlation with disease severity while ITM2A also demonstrated significant association with UC severity (Fig. 5A). Both proteins were significantly elevated in UC compared to HC and AD (Fig. 5B). The combined protein model effectively distinguished individuals with UC from HCs, achieving an AUC of 0.91 ± 0.05 (Fig. 5C).

To assess potential treatment-related confounding, we conducted sensitivity analysis on disease-differentiating proteins excluding patients who received systemic therapies. Although statistical power was reduced due to the smaller sample size following exclusion, the overall directional trends were preserved across groups, suggesting that the identified disease-associated proteomic signatures were unlikely to be primarily driven by treatment exposure (Supplementary Fig. 6).

Correlation heatmap reveals an AD-specific protein module
Next, we aimed to identify groups of proteins with highly correlated expression within each disease group. To determine disease-specific protein modules relevant to disease activity, we performed Pearson correlation analysis between two protein expression levels. The following inclusion criteria were applied: proteins identified as upregulated through DEP analysis, protein-protein correlations with statistical significance (P values ranging from 0.001 to 0.05), and proteins highly correlated with LY6D, which had the highest importance score. The analysis identified an AD protein module consisting of four proteins, CD70, CDON, IL-32 and LY6D (Fig. 6A, Supplementary Table 6). Among these proteins, LY6D, CDON and CD70, were highly correlated with disease severity suggesting disease-specific biomarkers. On the other hand, correlations among the proteins in the AD protein module were markedly weaker in HC (Fig. 6B, Supplementary Table 7). These results highlighted an AD-specific protein module with strong correlations in protein expression levels that may reflect specific biological mechanisms involved in inflammation.

DISCUSSION
AD and UC are representative chronic inflammatory diseases of the skin and gut, respectively, both involving immune dysregulation and barrier dysfunction. While both diseases primarily affect distinct lesional sites, we investigated the systemic profile of AD and UC using plasma proteomic profiling, as systemic immune activation is also a shared feature. Our study aimed to elucidate their systemic proteomic profiles and unique molecular pathways by identifying disease-differentiating biomarkers to provide insights into disease-specific inflammatory pathways.

Integration of an ML approach selected disease-differentiating proteins and the predictive power for disease classification was assessed. The disease classification model composed of ML-selected proteins demonstrated high discriminative power, ranging from 0.96, 0.99 to 1.00 in each cohort. The importance score of proteins helped distinguish disease-differentiating biomarkers. The ML-selected proteins were mainly involved in immune system (CASP2, CCL13, CCL26, CD40, CD70, IL-32, LY6D, MZB1, PIK3AP1, SIT1 and WAS), enzymatic regulation and degradation (GAL, PSMG3 and REG4), metabolism (ADA, CKTM1A/CKMT1B, FABP1, KYNU and MVK), intracellular transport (ITM2A and RAB6A), and angiogenesis and tissue remodeling (ANGPT-1, CDON and MMP1).

We also investigated groups of proteins that were correlated with disease severity. In AD, six proteins -CCL13, CCL26, CD70, CDON, LY6D and MMP1- were positively correlated with EASI scores. CCL13 and CCL26 are chemokines that attract eosinophils associated with the Th2 inflammatory response and are known to be elevated in AD patients.16171819202122 Moreover, MMP1, or matrix metalloproteinase 1, is a zinc-dependent endopeptidase that degrades collagen and plays a significant role in pathological tissue remodeling.23 Notably, it has been observed to be upregulated in serum and skin lesions of AD, and its expression progressively decreases during dupilumab treatment, leading to suppression of other T-helper pathways.232425

Interestingly, CD70, CDON and LY6D have been minimally studied in the context of AD. CD70, a tumor necrosis factor ligand, plays a critical role in T-cell activation and survival through its interaction with CD27.2627 Studies have shown that CD70 expression on B cells in combination with IL-4 enhances IgE synthesis, and its downregulation on the surface of Langerhans cells, together with decreased IL-12 production in MC903-treated mice, likely plays a pivotal role in driving the polarized Th2 cytokine response observed in MC903-treated mice.2829 LY6D, also known as lymphocyte antigen 6D, is essential in the early stages of lymphocyte specification and development.29 It has been reported that knockdown of filaggrin (FLG) can disrupt LY6D, suggesting FLG deficiency might contribute to atopy even without involvement of immune cells.30 In addition, CDON, or cell adhesion molecule/down-regulated by oncogenes, is a glycoprotein involved in cell-cell interactions and plays a vital role in various developmental processes.3132 It has been reported to enhance Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) signaling, which promotes neurogenesis and is associated with the severity of AD.3334 While several proteins in the identified signature (CCL13, CCL26 and MMP1) have been previously implicated in AD, others such as CDON, CD70 and LY6D have been minimally studied in this context, suggesting potential new biological insights that warrant further investigation.

In UC, REG4 and ITM2A were significantly correlated with disease severity, highlighting their potential roles in gut inflammation and tissue repair. REG4, or regenerating islet-derived protein 4, is associated with the overactivation of the STAT3 signaling pathway implicated in tissue protection and mucosal repair.35 Previous studies showed upregulated levels of REG4 in UC tissues, particularly in inflamed epithelium, dysplastic regions, cancerous lesions, and in the serum of patients with intestinal failure.3637 On the other hand, ITM2A, integral membrane protein 2A, is a membrane protein involved in immune cell adhesion, T-cell activation and the release of inflammatory mediators.3839

We also investigated groups of proteins with shared and specific biological mechanism that may be involved in disease pathogenesis. Pearson correlation analysis of protein expression levels identified a distinct AD-specific module consisting of CD70, CDON, IL-32 and LY6D. These protein modules provide insights into proteins that are highly correlated and exhibit coordinated expression patterns. IL-32, a cytokine produced by T cells, NK cells, and monocytes, activates JAK1 signaling and contributes to the pathogenesis of AD.40 Interestingly, the IL-32γ isoform has been shown to reduce disease severity in MC903-induced AD mouse models.41 IL-32 and CD70 emerged as strongly correlated proteins, suggesting their direct involvement in T cell activation and inflammatory responses, while CDON and LY6D may link lymphocyte development and cell signaling.

The study has several limitations. First, the study profiled a limited number of proteins in plasma samples collected at a single time point. Assessing a greater number of proteins or including longitudinal samples could have provided additional insights into protein-protein correlations and disease progression. The role of the identified disease-specific modules in active lesional tissue remains to be investigated. Also, this study was limited to Korean patients, and further studies may be needed to generalize our findings of disease-differentiating biomarkers. In addition, although several proteins showed statistically significant correlations with disease severity, the observed correlation coefficients were in the moderate range (r ≈ 0.4–0.6). Therefore, the severity-related biomarkers identified in this study should be interpreted as modestly associated with clinical severity, and further validation in larger, independent cohorts is required to determine their clinical utility and reproducibility.

Additionally, treatment-related confounding represents an additional limitation. A subset of patients was receiving systemic immunomodulatory therapies at the time of blood collection, and individual clinical requirements determined treatment initiation and duration, which could not be uniformly controlled. Although post-hoc analyses did not demonstrate major proteomic shifts attributable to specific medications, the small sample sizes within treatment subgroups limit definitive conclusions. Furthermore, as longitudinal sampling was not available, future studies incorporating treatment-naive cohorts and longitudinal proteomic profiling will be important to more rigorously assess the impact of therapeutic exposure on plasma protein signatures.

Despite the model’s notable discriminatory performance in our dataset, it remains unknown whether it can be applied to larger patient populations. The sample size was modest relative to the number of profiled proteins, which may increase the risk of overfitting despite the use of nested cross-validation and penalized regression. Although strict separation of training and testing folds was applied to minimize data leakage, internal validation cannot fully replace validation in an independent cohort. To confirm reproducibility, evaluate robustness, and generalizability of the identified 24-protein signature across a range of patient demographics and disease severities, future research should incorporate large sample sizes and external validation datasets. Our approach could be further applied to other inflammatory diseases and other contexts.

In summary, we have uncovered complex proteomic signatures of AD and UC and proposed disease-differentiating protein modules. Through plasma proteomic profiling, ML modeling, and correlation analyses of protein expression with disease severity as well as among proteins with correlated modules, this study outlines disease-differentiating protein modules and suggests AD-specific biomarkers that may improve diagnosis and guide targeted treatments.

paper.title: Suture stem cells in pediatric craniosynostosis: pathophysiological mechanisms, surgical management, and emerging regenerative therapies.
paper.abstract: Craniosynostosis (CS) is a complex congenital disorder characterized by the premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures resulting from interactions between genetic alterations, environmental influences, and the dysregulated differentiation of cranial suture stem cells (SuSCs). Increasing evidence indicates that SuSC homeostasis disruption, including alterations in glioma-associated oncogene homolog 1-positive, axis inhibition protein 2-positive, and other stem/progenitor cell populations, along with aberrant regulation of developmental signaling pathways, plays a central role in the pathogenesis of CS. This review summarizes current advances in SuSC biology and the molecular mechanisms of, diagnostic approaches for, and therapeutic strategies for CS. By integrating evidence from studies published in 2000-2026, we discuss how genetic mutations and signaling pathways, including the fibroblast growth factor, bone morphogenetic protein, Wnt, and Hedgehog pathways, influence SuSC maintenance, lineage commitment, and osteogenic differentiation. We further summarize recent clinical advances, including virtual surgical planning, three-dimensional printing, and endoscope-assisted minimally invasive techniques, as well as emerging molecular and stem cellbased regenerative strategies aimed at restoring functional cranial suture structures. By connecting genetic mechanisms, stem cell biology, and translational medicine, this review provides an integrated framework to increase our understanding of the pathogenesis of CS and highlights potential directions for the development of mechanism-based therapies to improve long-term craniofacial and neurodevelopmental outcomes.
